notes.title: Fundamentals of Agentic AI
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: This course covers the fundamentals of Agentic AI across seven classes, starting with code and programming, moving through software systems, machine learning foundations, deep learning, and finally focusing on LLM behavior, prompting, and retrieval. The curriculum is structured to build practical skills, culminating in building working AI workflows.
DETAILS:
- Class 1: Code & Programming Foundations covers topics such as what code is, building blocks like variables and loops, programming languages (specifically Python), and tools like Claude Code and Codex [E2].
- Class 2: Software Systems — Frontend to Deployment covers topics including Frontend (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), Backend (servers, APIs), Databases (SQL), and deployment to a live URL, with Assignment 1 being building and deploying a networking tracker [E4].
- Class 3: Machine Learning Foundations covers concepts like AI history, defining predictions, fitting models by reducing loss, training digit classifiers in Colab, and reinforcement learning (e.g., Pac-Man) [E6].
- Class 4: Deep Learning, Embeddings & Transformers covers topics such as one neuron structure, network training (predict, measure loss, calculate gradients, update), and language concepts like tokens, embeddings, and attention [E8].
- Class 5: LLM Behavior, Prompting & Retrieval covers topics including prompting techniques, context management, fine-tuning, RLHF, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and Assignment 4, which is building a Personal Wiki CLI around local Gemma + RAG [E10].

notes.title: Class 1 - Code Foundations
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Class 1, Code & Programming Foundations, focuses on prototyping with AI to build internal tools, A/B tests, and dashboards rather than becoming a software developer. The class aims to equip students with the ability to read, explain, modify, and test small programs, using the mental model that a program is a precise recipe transforming inputs into outputs.
DETAILS:
- The goal of the class is to prototype with AI for things like internal tools, A/B tests, and dashboards [E1].
- Success in the class means being able to read a small program without panic, explain its inputs, changes, and returns, change one behavior deliberately, test the change, and run a website on one's own machine [E2].
- A program is conceptualized as a precise recipe that transforms inputs into outputs, while other elements like websites and models are elaborations of that recipe [E2].
- Key building blocks of all software, from Instagram to self-driving cars, are variables, conditionals, loops, and functions, with complexity arising from combining them [E4].
- The agenda includes topics such as what code is (recipes, binary), building blocks (variables, conditionals, loops, functions), errors as information, programming languages (why Python), the terminal, clean code, Git & GitHub, localhost, and tools like Claude Code, Codex, and YOLO mode [E3].
- The exercise involves building a business-rule engine, the discount-engine, which must run on the machine, be viewable in a browser, and be structured logically [E5].
- The definition of done for the discount-engine includes having a README, sensible structure, running on localhost in a browser, passing unit tests for rules, using plan mode, and pushing to GitHub with readable commit messages [E6].

notes.title: Class 2 - Software Systems
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Class 2, Software Systems, covers the process of turning a program into a product by detailing the product stack, including frontend, backend, databases, authentication, cloud deployment, and the assignment. This material outlines the steps from local testing to deploying a live, shareable application.
DETAILS:
- The process of moving from localhost testing to a real URL involves having a browser ask for a page and a machine answer it, where the difference is who is answering [E2].
- The frontend is what users interact with in a browser, while the backend is the machine that answers the request [E2].
- Databases provide the application's durable memory and fast temporary storage, and can include options like PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis [E5].
- Secrets and authentication are mechanisms that allow the system to know who is making a request [E2].
- Cloud and deployment describe how the application comes into existence [E2].
- A tech stack is defined as the combination of technologies used to build and run an application [E5].
- The assignment requires building a networking tracker using the stack: Next.js + Supabase + Vercel [E6].
- The definition of done includes having the app live on a public URL, supporting user sign-in/sign-out, ensuring data privacy between users, validating inputs, and having at least one automated test pass [E7].

notes.title: Class 3 - Machine Learning
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Class 3 covers machine learning foundations, focusing on how models are trained, the concept of generalization, evaluation, and the different learning paradigms including unsupervised and reinforcement learning, culminating in the Pac-Man project. It emphasizes that machine learning involves training a model on past usage and outcomes to predict future results.
DETAILS:
- Machine learning involves using past usage and renewal outcomes to train a learned model to predict renewal estimates for a new account [E1].
- Training fits the model’s settings by choosing the inputs and objective [E1].
- A learned model captures useful patterns from training examples in its parameters, allowing it to make predictions about new examples, provided the learned patterns still apply when the situation changes [E4].
- The process of AI history involves checking whether learning generalizes [E5].
- The route for AI history includes defining the prediction and preparing data, comparing models and evaluating errors, fitting a model by reducing loss, finding clusters without labels (unsupervised learning), choosing actions through reinforcement learning, and training a Grid World policy, then starting Pac-Man [E5].
- Three ways a machine can learn are Supervised learning (inputs + known answers to predict an answer), Unsupervised learning (inputs without answers to find structure), and Reinforcement learning (an environment + rewards to choose actions over time) [E6].
- The Pac-Man project involves training an agent to play Ms. Pac-Man by choosing exploration, episodes, and learning rate, and watching gameplay to compare before/after scores [E7].
- Evaluation for the Pac-Man project requires submitting a notebook with the three chosen hyperparameters, an untrained GIF, later checkpoints, a training plot, and a comparison of five evaluation games with the untrained baseline [E8].

notes.title: Class 4 - Deep Learning and Transformers
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Class 4 covers the progression from hand-designed features to learned representations using neural networks, embeddings, attention, and transformers, culminating in a tiny language model assignment. This material focuses on how deep learning learns intermediate features and how language models function as predictions.
DETAILS:
- Deep learning learns multiple layers of representation, where pixel values transform into simple patterns, combinations, and predictions [E4].
- A neural network functions by turning input numbers into output numbers using adjustable weights and biases, and training involves changing parameters to reduce loss on examples [E5].
- The roadmap for the class includes understanding one neuron, a network learning intermediate features, training by predicting and measuring loss, and exploring language concepts like tokens, embeddings, attention, and transformers [E6].
- Language model training rewards predicting text, and a confident prediction does not verify the answer, as it can produce plausible but incorrect facts [E7].
- The assignment requires choosing text, training a supplied tiny language model (using Karpathy’s nanoGPT in PyTorch), and explaining the changes using outputs [E8].
- During the assignment, one should inspect five examples from the corpus to explain what patterns they could teach [E9].
- Embeddings are learned vectors, and token IDs are lookup indices, while the corpus and IDs remain fixed during training, and training changes the learned parameters [E9].

notes.title: Class 5 - LLMs Prompting and Retrieval
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: This class covers LLM behavior, focusing on prompting techniques, context management, fine-tuning, and retrieval methods like RAG. It emphasizes practical application for building AI workflows rather than deep ML engineering, addressing concepts like hallucination and the role of different model behaviors.
DETAILS:
- Prompting is used to steer the probability distribution, potentially with or without thinking mode, to achieve useful answers initially [E1].
- Context management addresses why models forget, the role of compaction, and how this limits AI features [E1].
- Fine-tuning and RLHF are processes labs perform to make a base model an assistant, impacting design choices like "Anthropic values" [E1].
- Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) allows bolting company data onto a general model without retraining, contrasting with the model's frozen training data [E1, E6].
- Prompt engineering involves techniques such as using .md files, system prompts, and CLAUDE.md, following a "golden rule" [E2].
- Thinking models are used when a model plans before generating a response [E2].
- Hallucination can be mitigated by RAG retrieving evidence and citing sources, or by using higher thinking modes, though higher modes increase computation costs [E5].
- Fine-tuning changes the model, while prompting changes instructions and examples, and retrieval finds relevant material as context without updating model weights [E3].

notes.title: Networking Tracker
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: The Networking Tracker is a private contact tracker designed for users at Berkeley, allowing each signed-in user to maintain isolated contact lists with features for adding, editing, sorting, and filtering contacts. It emphasizes security through Row Level Security within Postgres and uses a modern stack including Next.js 16, TypeScript, and Neon services.
DETAILS:
- User data isolation is achieved via Row Level Security inside Postgres, where the database filters rows based on the caller's identity extracted from a signed JWT, preventing users from seeing other users' data even if they bypass the application. [E1]
- Accounts are managed using Email + password sign-up, sign-in, and sign-out via Neon Managed Better Auth, with sessions held in an `HttpOnly`, signed cookie. [E2]
- Contacts can be added with fields for name, company, role, where met, notes, and priority, with priority constrained to `high`, `medium`, or `low` in three independent places. [E2]
- The technology stack includes Next.js 16 (App Router) and TypeScript for separating frontend and backend, Tailwind CSS v4 with Radix UI primitives for styling, and Zod for validation. [E3]
- Security relies on Row Level Security on the `contacts` table with four separate policies, ensuring `user_id` defaults to `auth.user_id()` and that `UPDATE` policies use `WITH CHECK` to prevent reassignment of rows. [E2]
- Testing involves `Vitest` to run the real route handler with the database mocked, verifying validation contracts (25 tests) and API contract order of operations (5 tests), which confirms that inserted rows do not contain a `user_id` from the client. [E4]
- The application is hosted on Vercel, which provides first-class Next.js support and a public HTTPS URL with zero configuration. [E3]

notes.title: Pac-Man DQN Agent
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: The Pac-Man DQN Agent was trained on Atari Ms. Pac-Man using three specific settings: exploration at 0.10, 300 episodes, and a learning rate of 0.0001. This run showed a mean evaluation score increase from 492.0 to 604.0, but the learning was described as limited and noisy.
DETAILS:
- The training budget consisted of 300 episodes, which took approximately 1,996 s (about 33 min, including periodic demos) and resulted in 173,434 decisions [E7].
- The exploration setting was set to 0.10, which is close to the final exploration level in standard DQN, allowing the agent to try new routes while maintaining 10% random training play [E2].
- The learning rate was set to 0.0001, which is the standard, stable Adam learning rate for DQN [E2].
- The mean evaluation score went from 492.0 (untrained) to 604.0 (trained) across five evaluation games [E1, E4].
- A limitation noted is that evaluation is small and noisy, as the +112.0 improvement came almost entirely from one game (seed 303), and three games scored lower after training [E8].
- The next experiment planned is to change only the number of episodes from 300 to 1,000, keeping exploration at 0.10 and the learning rate at 0.0001 [E9].

notes.title: Tiny nanoGPT Model
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: The Tiny nanoGPT Model refers to two word-level models trained from scratch using the nanoGPT framework, which are used to evaluate language understanding based on corpus size. These models are characterized by specific settings and are tested against a fixed 48-case language evaluation suite.
DETAILS:
- Both tiny word-level nanoGPT models were trained from scratch with 2 blocks, 4 heads, 64-number embeddings, and a 48-token context [E1].
- The two models used the same settings, with only the corpus differing between the Starter (classroom corpus only) and Expanded (classroom corpus plus teaching files for opposites and spatial relations) versions [E1].
- The training steps for both models were set to 3,000 [E3].
- The Starter model achieved 19 correct out of 48 cases (39.6% correct) after training, while the Expanded model achieved 29 correct out of 48 cases (60.4% correct) [E2].
- The Expanded model had a vocabulary of 358 (355 types, under the 509 cap), compared to 136 for the Starter model [E4].
- The training split for both experiments was 4,132 / 460 passages (90/10 by passage, seed 42) [E4].
- The chat interface allows interaction with the expanded model, which is noted as a tiny model that continues short sentences and is not a general assistant [E1].

notes.title: Personal Wiki Project
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: The Personal Wiki Project is a Class 5 assignment requiring the development of a personal wiki powered by a local model, retrieval, and chat/ask/search modes. This project involves building a wiki from personal notes using local Gemma and RAG, and creating a CLI to interact with the system.
DETAILS:
- The personal wiki must consist of 3+ original notes with readable note names, topic groups, and meaningful links in Obsidian [E2].
- The personal CLI should allow users to chat to brainstorm, ask for cited answers, and search original passages [E2].
- The system must support a chat function that acts as a personal assistant with conversation context and retrieval when needed [E2].
- The 'ask' function provides standalone factual answers with evidence and citations, or states if evidence is missing [E2].
- The search function returns original passages and source locations without generating an answer [E2].
- The project requires testing with 3 answerable questions and 1 unsupported question, plus chat and search checks [E2].
- The project must be runnable offline by disconnecting the internet and restarting the CLI to record ingestion and tests [E2].
- The README must explain setup, model and runtime choice, device specs, measured memory and response time, architecture, test results, and one limitation with a proposed improvement [E2].

notes.title: Git and GitHub
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Git is a version control system that tracks every change to every file in a project, while GitHub is a cloud service that hosts Git repositories, enabling collaboration through features like Pull Requests. This system solves the problem of tracking changes, allowing users to go back in time and work on the same project simultaneously.
DETAILS:
- Git is a version control system that keeps a complete history of every change to every file [E2].
- A commit is defined as a snapshot of a project at a specific point in time and is a named, reviewable claim about a coherent change [E2].
- A branch is a parallel version of a project used for experimentation without affecting the main version [E2].
- A repository (repo) is a project folder tracked by Git, containing code files, the full history of changes in the .git/ folder, and configuration files [E5].
- A diff shows exactly what has changed, with red lines indicating removals and green lines indicating additions, and this view is constantly seen in pull requests [E3].
- GitHub hosts Git repositories in the cloud, providing remote storage, collaboration capabilities, and features like Pull Requests and Issues [E6].
- The Git workflow involves steps such as pulling the latest changes, creating a branch, writing code, staging changes with git add, saving a snapshot with git commit, uploading to GitHub with git push, opening a Pull Request for review, and finally merging to main [E8].
- A Pull Request is a proposed change accompanied by a description, diff, review comments, automated checks, and a merge button, serving as an audit trail for changes [E11].

notes.title: Localhost and Ports
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Localhost and ports are concepts related to running software on a machine, where localhost refers to the machine itself via the address 127.0.0.1, and ports act as identifiers for specific programs running on that machine. This setup is crucial because a website is a running process, and localhost links only work on the local machine, not over the internet.
DETAILS:
- localhost is a name that always points back at the machine you are typing on, with the address 127.0.0.1, meaning "this computer" [E2].
- localhost requests, such as http://localhost:8000, never touch the internet; the request goes from the browser to another program on the same laptop and returns [E2].
- Ports function as apartment numbers for one address, indicating which program is being talked to; for example, localhost:8000 might be a Python’s built-in web server, while localhost:3000 might be a Node / React / Next.js dev server [E3].
- The address is the building, and the port is the apartment; if an address is already in use, a different port must be used or the program must be stopped [E3].
- Running a web server locally involves a process that starts and keeps running, waiting for requests, and each new line in the terminal log represents a request made by the browser [E1, E5].
- A website is a process that must be running on a computer that is on; if the terminal is stopped (e.g., by Ctrl+C), the site cannot be reached even if the file remains on disk [E7].
- localhost is not the internet; sending a localhost URL to someone else results in a connection error because the address points only to the local machine [E8].
- Localhost is used for testing, but it cannot be shared with others because the address points to the user's machine, not a public address [E10].

notes.title: Clean Code
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Clean Code focuses on readability and maintainability by emphasizing principles like guard clauses, named constants, single-responsibility functions, and splitting projects by responsibility. These practices ensure that code is easier for teammates and AI agents to read and modify, which is crucial because code is read far more often than it is written.
DETAILS:
- Readability is important because code is read dozens of times by teammates and AI agents after being written [E1].
- The WTF-per-Minute Metric is a social metric measuring the gap between what the code does and what a reader expected it to do, which can only be measured by a second human [E2].
- Spaghetti Code is dangerous because it forces the reader to ask questions about variables, constants, nesting, and logic, leading to future bugs [E4].
- Guard Clauses beat nesting because handling exceptional cases first allows the rest of the function to represent the normal path, avoiding deep nesting [E6].
- Magic Numbers should be replaced with named constants (e.g., COLLECTIONS_CUTOFF_DAYS) so that each number explicitly states what it represents, making changes clearer [E7].
- One Function, One Job means splitting functions so that a function performs only one task, allowing for easier testing and reuse [E8].
- Comments should explain why a decision was made (a record of a decision) rather than restating what the code already shows, as good names remove the need for "what" comments [E9].
- A project is best treated as a folder rather than a single file, as opening a folder allows agents to understand the layout and follow imports across files [E11].
- Splitting by Responsibility means organizing files so that each file answers one kind of question, making it easier to pinpoint where a change belongs [E12].

notes.title: AI Coding Agents
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: AI Coding Agents are tools like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex that run in the terminal, capable of reading codebases, writing files, and running commands autonomously. They are powerful but require human oversight, especially regarding code quality and accountability.
DETAILS:
- Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are AI agents that operate in the terminal rather than as browser chatbots [E2].
- Both Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can read codebases, write files, run commands, and iterate autonomously [E2].
- The CLI is considered the most powerful version of agents because it offers full filesystem access, command execution capabilities, and autonomous iteration [E3].
- YOLO Mode allows agents like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to skip permission prompts, meaning they create files, install packages, and run commands without prior user confirmation, suitable for greenfield projects [E4].
- Plan Mode involves typing `/plan` in Claude Code to describe a desired build, allowing the AI to create a detailed plan for review before execution, which can then be run in YOLO mode [E5].
- When using an agent, it is important to slow down for decisions requiring context (like technology choices) or when dealing with production data, and to verify outputs by running tests [E6].
- Before accepting an agent's diff, a checklist should be used to verify if the change matches the brief, check for unexpected files, look for secrets, and ensure tests still pass [E9].

notes.title: APIs and HTTP
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: APIs function as agreements between systems, defining what callers can send and rely on receiving, while HTTP methods communicate the intent of those interactions. This interaction is typically structured using JSON for data exchange and is governed by status codes that summarize the outcome of the request.
DETAILS:
- APIs are described using the Waiter Metaphor where the Waiter acts as the API, the kitchen is the backend, and the fridge is the database [E1].
- An API serves as an Agreement Between Systems, specifying what callers can send and what they can rely on receiving, with version contracts deliberately used to prevent breaking consumers [E2].
- HTTP methods communicate intent: GET is for reading data, POST is for creating data, PUT is for updating data, and DELETE is for removing data, with PATCH allowing changes to part of a resource [E3].
- JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the language of APIs, providing a simple text format for sending data between machines [E4].
- Never trust incoming API requests; the backend must validate types, ranges, permissions, and allowed fields because untrusted input could lead to privilege escalation or identity takeover [E5].
- Status codes are part of the contract, where 2xx indicates success, 4xx indicates the caller sent a bad request, and 5xx indicates the server failed [E6].
- An HTTP Request is structured text containing the method, path, host, authorization, content type, and a body payload [E7].
- The process of updating a contact's priority involves the browser sending a PATCH request, which is validated against schemas, and the database performing ownership checks before executing the update [E8].

notes.title: Databases and SQL
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Databases organize records by defining a place for every record, where a database acts as an organized warehouse, and tables store facts while relationships connect them. SQL is the language used to query this data, and the structure of these databases is crucial for application memory and data modeling.
DETAILS:
- A database is conceptualized as an organized warehouse where every kind of record has a defined place and a reliable way to find it [E1].
- A table stores facts, and rows follow the same columns, while different entities reside in separate tables [E2].
- Relationships connect rows through IDs, and together the tables and their links form the data model, which is a map for design before coding [E2].
- SQL (Structured Query Language) is the method used to ask a database for data, allowing operations like selecting all users, filtering by role, counting users by role, and sorting by name [E4].
- For large-data work, the data stack suggests pushing filtering, joining, sorting, and aggregating work down the stack to the database layer [E5].
- The `public.contacts` table in the Networking Tracker schema includes columns such as `id` (a primary key), `user_id` (a `text` column that is `not null` and defaults to `auth.user_id()`), `name`, `company`, `role`, `where_met`, `notes`, `priority`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` [E10].
- The `user_id` column is defined as `not null` because an unauthenticated caller cannot insert a row, and it defaults to `auth.user_id()` to ensure every row has an owner [E11].

notes.title: Authentication and Sessions
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Authentication is crucial because without it, anyone can access any user's data, and it answers the question of whether a user is who they claim to be. This process involves a specific flow where the browser signs in, a session cookie is set, and a JWT is used to verify identity with the database.
DETAILS:
- Without authentication, anyone can access anyone’s data, and the app has no idea who is making a request [E1].
- Authentication answers the question: “Are you who you say you are?” [E1].
- Building a prototype without authentication means every user can see every other user’s data, which is the #1 mistake in vibecoded apps [E1].
- The user signs in by posting to `/api/auth/sign-in/email` on the app's own origin [E3].
- This route proxies to Neon Managed Better Auth using the server-only cookie secret, setting an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, signed session cookie that JavaScript cannot read [E3].
- When the backend needs to query data, it exchanges the session for a short-lived JWT via `auth.token()` [E3].
- The JWT travels to the Neon Data API as a `Bearer` token, and Neon verifies its signature against Neon Auth's JWKS rather than taking the app's word for who the user is [E3].
- Inside Postgres, `auth.user_id()` returns the verified `sub` claim [E3].
- The app never tells the database who the user is; it hands over a token the database checks for itself [E3].

notes.title: Row Level Security
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Row Level Security (RLS) in the Networking Tracker isolates each user's rows by implementing four policies for select, insert, update, and delete operations. This mechanism relies on the distinction between `USING` and `WITH CHECK` clauses to control row filtering and validation during data access.
DETAILS:
- The `user_id` column is defined with a `default (auth.user_id())` and `not null` constraint, meaning the application never sends `user_id` on insert, and unauthenticated callers cannot insert because `auth.user_id()` returns `NULL`. [E1]
- The four policies implemented are `contacts_select_own`, `contacts_insert_own`, `contacts_update_own`, and `contacts_delete_own`. [E2]
- The `USING` clause filters rows that already exist, determining which rows may be read, updated, or deleted. [E2]
- The `WITH CHECK` clause validates rows as they will be after a write operation to ensure the result still belongs to the user. [E2]
- `UPDATE` policies require both `USING` and `WITH CHECK` to prevent a user from changing a row so it belongs to someone else. [E2]
- `INSERT` policies only use `WITH CHECK` because there is no pre-existing row to filter. [E2]
- `SELECT` and `DELETE` policies only use `USING` because they do not produce a new row. [E2]
- `GRANT` determines if the `authenticated` role can issue the statement, while RLS decides which rows are returned. [E2]
- `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is used to remove the default exemption where table owners bypass RLS, ensuring nothing runs unfiltered. [E2]

notes.title: Secrets and Environment Variables
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Secrets and environment variables concern the practice of keeping sensitive information out of code, detailing which environment variables are public or server-only and the rationale behind this separation. This is important because hard-coding secrets or shipping them in frontend code allows attackers to compromise accounts or access data.
DETAILS:
- The safe pattern for local secrets is to store them in `.env.local` [E1].
- In production, secrets should use your cloud provider’s environment settings, and the backend should read secrets at runtime [E1].
- Never commit `.env` files or put secret keys in frontend code [E1].
- Environment variables like `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_DATA_API_URL` are public by design because they are addresses, not credentials [E2].
- `NEON_AUTH_BASE_URL` and `NEON_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` are not exposed to the browser [E2].
- `DATABASE_URL` is not exposed because it is a credential that names a role and password and would bypass the Data API entirely [E2].
- `NEON_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET` requires a minimum of 32 characters and should be generated with `openssl rand -hex 32` [E2].

notes.title: Testing and CI
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Testing and CI in JD's work focuses on treating tests as executable promises, using CI/CD as a release gate, and employing strategies like regression tests and the test pyramid. This approach is demonstrated through specific test suites and validation contracts.
DETAILS:
- Tests turn examples into executable promises, such as writing an example as a test if a policy dictates a 15% strategic customer discount [E1].
- Regression tests catch distant breakage by rerunning the full suite after every change, catching failures far from the modified code [E2].
- The Test Pyramid suggests many fast unit tests for small decisions, fewer integration checks for system boundaries, and a few end-to-end checks for the user's real path [E3].
- Unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint failures, while end-to-end tests take minutes and only indicate "something broke somewhere" [E3].
- The `tests/validation.test.ts` file contains 25 tests verifying rules such as rejecting empty or whitespace-only names, trimming valid names, and rejecting invalid priority values like `urgent`, `HIGH`, `""`, `1`, `critical`, and a missing value [E4].
- The `tests/api-contract.test.ts` file contains 5 tests asserting the order of operations for the `POST /api/contacts` handler, including checks for signed-out users, empty names, invalid priorities, and ensuring no `user_id` is sent upstream for a valid contact [E4].
- The latest run of tests shows 30 tests passed in total, consisting of 25 from `tests/validation.test.ts` and 5 from `tests/api-contract.test.ts` [E4].

notes.title: Cloud Deployment
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Cloud deployment involves moving a tested version of code into an environment, which requires managing different environments and planning for rollbacks. This process is demonstrated by deploying a full-stack web app using a stack like Next.js, Supabase, and Vercel.
DETAILS:
- The cloud is defined as someone else’s computers in a data center, allowing users to rent computing power instead of buying and maintaining servers [E1].
- Deployment is the process of moving a tested version into an environment [E9].
- Environments are intentionally different places, with Development using local fake/local data and Production using real users and real credentials [E9].
- Secrets should be stored in server-only environment settings for production, and the backend should read secrets at runtime, never exposing them to the frontend [E4].
- On Vercel, deploying involves adding a new project by importing the repository and accepting auto-detected Next.js settings [E11].
- Rollback on Vercel is achieved by promoting a previous deployment, which is described as a one-click action [E10].
- For the networking tracker assignment, deployment involves pushing the repository to GitHub, adding environment variables (like `NEXT_PUBLIC_NEON_AUTH_URL`) in Vercel settings, and applying the schema SQL [E11].

notes.title: Model Training and Gradient Descent
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Model training involves adjusting adjustable parameters of a model to fit historical examples by minimizing a loss function, often using gradient descent to iteratively improve predictions. This process starts with a poor guess and repeats updates until the loss converges, which is how a model learns from data.
DETAILS:
- A model has adjustable parameters, such as slope \(w\) and intercept \(b\), which are chosen during training to fit historical examples [E1].
- Training involves choosing parameter values that fit historical examples [E1].
- Loss measures prediction error, and training tries to reduce this average; for toy revenue data, the mean squared error is approximately 12.7 [E2].
- Training starts with predictions that miss most observations [E3].
- Adjusting the line involves changing the slope and intercept to reduce loss, which can improve the fit but may still result in missed observations [E4].
- Repeated updates improve the fit as errors get smaller, with the loss dropping from 312 to 58 [E5].
- Gradient descent updates parameters by predicting, measuring loss, computing the gradient, taking a small downhill step, and repeating, where the learning rate controls the step size [E7].
- Training and inference use different information: training uses historical features and known answers to update parameters, while inference uses features for a new case and the fitted model's parameters [E12].

notes.title: Overfitting and Generalization
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Overfitting and generalization relate to how a model fits training data, where overfitting occurs when a model fits training details that do not generalize, and bias and variance describe the systematic error and model flexibility, respectively. This concept is important when using test sets, validation data, and baselines to guide model development and ensure future predictions are reliable.
DETAILS:
- Overfitting occurs when a model fits training details that do not carry over [E3].
- Underfitting is when the model is too limited to capture the pattern [E3].
- Bias is defined as the systematic error from simplifying assumptions, while variance is how much the fitted model changes with the training sample [E4].
- Validation data can be used to choose settings and can guide development, but the final test set should remain untouched until choices are fixed [E1, E2].
- For future predictions, training should be done on older cases, validation on later ones, and testing on the newest held-out period [E2].
- The loss from the two experiments (Starter and Expanded) cannot be compared because they use different corpora and vocabularies [E6].
- Validation loss staying close to training loss rules out heavy memorization of individual sentences, but it does not show generalization beyond the same templates [E6].

notes.title: Precision and Recall
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Precision and Recall are metrics used to count different types of mistakes made by a model, which is important because accuracy alone can hide errors depending on the cost associated with different types of errors. These metrics help in understanding the trade-offs between false positives and false negatives.
DETAILS:
- True Positives (TP) occur when the model correctly predicts the positive class, such as catching spam [E1].
- False Negatives (FN) occur when the model misses a positive case, such as a missed spam email [E1].
- False Positives (FP) occur when the model incorrectly predicts the positive class, such as a job offer going to spam [E1].
- Precision is calculated as the ratio of true positives to the total number of flagged predictions [E3].
- Recall is calculated as the ratio of true positives to the total number of actual positive cases [E3].
- A false positive can hide an important message for a spam filter, while a missed positive can carry a different cost for fraud detection [E1].
- A decision policy must be made based on the model output, such as deciding what action to take for a high fraud score [E5].

notes.title: Reinforcement Learning
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Reinforcement Learning is a learning method where an agent learns a policy from experience and rewards to optimize its behavior. It involves defining states, actions, and rewards, and the objective is to maximize the expected cumulative reward rather than just the immediate reward.
DETAILS:
- State is where the agent is now, and Action is the move it chooses [E1].
- Reward is feedback received after acting [E1].
- In Reinforcement Learning, the agent learns a policy from experience and rewards [E1].
- The objective is the expected cumulative reward, not the biggest reward on the next move [E2].
- Credit assignment is the process of determining which earlier action helped make a later outcome possible [E2].
- Q-Learning stores a value, $Q(s,a)$, which estimates the total discounted reward from a choice, used to follow the best-known choices [E3].
- The Reward Defines What the Agent Optimizes, as the agent learns based on the reward structure provided [E7].

notes.title: Deep Q-Networks
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Deep Q-Networks (DQN) use a neural network to estimate action values, replacing the traditional Q-table, allowing the agent to handle vast state spaces by processing input frames. This method utilizes components like frame stacking, experience replay, and a target network to stabilize training and improve learning efficiency.
DETAILS:
- DQN uses a neural network in place of the Q-table to estimate $Q(s,a)$ based on input frames [E1].
- Pac-Man DQN observes the last four game screens, shrunk to 84 × 84 grayscale, to determine movement [E3].
- The agent selects one of 9 joystick moves (no-op, up, right, left, down, and four diagonals), holding each choice for 4 game frames [E3].
- Rewards are clipped to be between −1 and +1 during training, meaning the agent learns "points or no points" [E3].
- Experience replay samples past transitions to reduce correlation and reuse experience [E2].
- A target network provides a slower-changing target for value updates [E2].
- Evaluation is small and noisy, and the agent can be unstable, with performance varying significantly across games [E4].

notes.title: Neural Networks
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Neural Networks are small calculations inspired by biological neurons that receive inputs, multiply them by weights, add a bias, and pass the result through an activation function to produce an output score. They are crucial because stacking these units allows models to combine features, and the training process involves adjusting parameters and hyperparameters to learn from data.
DETAILS:
- An artificial neuron receives inputs, multiplies each input by its weight, adds the results, and adds a bias before applying an activation function [E1].
- The formula for a neuron is output = activation(weight₁ × input₁ + weight₂ × input₂ + bias), where weights control input influence, bias shifts the calculation, and activation bends the response [E3].
- Weights control how an input changes a neuron's calculation, and they can be positive, negative, or near zero [E3].
- The bias shifts the calculation, similar to an intercept in a regression [E3].
- The activation function bends the response, and the result is passed to the next layer [E3].
- One neuron produces one feature, and connecting many neurons allows the model to combine features [E1].
- A single neuron's output score is passed through a sigmoid function, resulting in a score between 0 and 1 [E2].
- The network learns parameters, which include connection weights and neuron biases, such as the 26 learned parameters in a small network [E10, E11].
- Hyperparameters chosen for training include the number of layers and neurons, the activation function, the learning rate, and the training duration [E11].
- The training loop involves a forward pass, loss calculation, backward pass, and update step, where only the update step changes the parameters [E9].
- Backpropagation calculates how a small change to each setting would change the loss, and the optimizer uses these gradients to adjust the weights and biases [E8].
- Parameters are adjusted by choosing a connection and moving its weight, while the input data remains fixed [E10].

notes.title: Training Loss Curves
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Training loss curves in Pac-Man DQN showed that lower loss does not equate to better results, as loss can increase while performance fluctuates. Similarly, for nanoGPT, loss flattening indicates that the model has reached a point where further loss reduction is not possible, and losses from different experiments cannot be directly compared.
DETAILS:
- In Pac-Man DQN, the training loss climbed from about 0.02 to about 0.10–0.16 and ended near 0.09, demonstrating that lower loss is not the same as better play [E1].
- For Pac-Man DQN, the periodic single-game demo showed the agent's quality swung from one checkpoint to the next, with the episode-125 checkpoint looking stronger on one game than the final model [E1].
- In nanoGPT, the training-panel loss fell by about 86% by the halfway point and then flattened, which is expected because classroom sentences have slots filled at random [E5].
- For nanoGPT, validation loss stayed close to training loss, suggesting that heavy memorization of individual sentences is not occurring [E5].
- The losses from the two nanoGPT experiments cannot be compared because they use different corpora and vocabularies [E5].
- The 3× learning rate in nanoGPT gave no visible instability at the three measurement points [E5].

notes.title: Evaluation Design
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Evaluation design involves using fixed seeds and evaluation suites, testing with small noisy samples, and utilizing public development tests to assess model performance. This process is used to determine necessary changes to the model's training parameters.
DETAILS:
- For Pac-Man DQN, evaluation involved comparing results across five games with different seeds, showing a mean improvement from 492.0 to 604.0 after 300 episodes [E1].
- Evaluation is limited because the samples are small and noisy, and the agent is unstable, meaning five games cannot reliably distinguish real learning from luck [E2].
- To test the impact of training budget, the number of episodes was changed from 300 to 1,000 while keeping exploration at 0.10 and the learning rate at 0.0001 [E3].
- Public development tests were used for nanoGPT, and these tests were read to select extension categories, meaning they do not represent an unseen final benchmark [E4].
- For nanoGPT, the model's knowledge is tied to template slots, and new frames interfere with old ones, as seen in chat replies blending contrast frames into sentences [E5].
- A next experiment for nanoGPT involves adding a held-out set of new spatial and opposites prompts and running with 3 seeds per corpus to check if gains are a real pattern [E5].

notes.title: Tokens and Embeddings
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Tokens are pieces into which text is broken by a tokenizer, and embeddings are learned vectors that represent words or tokens in a high-dimensional space. These embeddings allow words to be compared mathematically based on their learned relationships and contexts.
DETAILS:
- An embedding is a learned vector (a list of numbers) that represents a word or token, and training adjusts these numbers to help the model make predictions [E1].
- Words in similar contexts tend to have similar embeddings, and words with similar meanings cluster together in vector space [E2].
- An embedding represents a word as a vector, and nearby vectors can capture related meanings; for example, "Dog" and "puppy" have related meanings, so their vectors are close together [E3].
- Distance between vectors measures similarity, where a smaller distance represents greater similarity, such as the distance from "dog" to "puppy" being $\sqrt{1.25}$ [E3].
- Context determines meaning, and modern models create contextual representations where the vector for a word is adjusted on the fly by the surrounding words via the attention mechanism [E4].
- A tokenizer breaks text into pieces called tokens, and BPE (byte-pair encoding) learns which pieces to combine [E5].
- A token ID is a lookup index that selects a row in the model’s learned embedding table, and a single word can be represented by multiple tokens [E5].
- Real embedding vectors usually contain many more numbers, and different tokenizers may produce different splits and token counts for the same text [E5].

notes.title: Transformer Attention
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Transformer Attention is a mechanism that allows a model to combine information from available token positions, replacing the sequential processing of RNNs. It enables attention to connect directly to earlier positions within the context window, allowing a word's representation to change based on the surrounding context.
DETAILS:
- Attention combines information from the token positions available to the current position [E5].
- Attention can connect directly to earlier positions within the context window [E5].
- A word's starting embedding is shared, but its representation changes as the network combines it with available context [E8].
- Attention updates the embedding for a token by pulling it toward a meaning based on its context (e.g., "American shrew" pulls "mole" toward the animal direction) [E9].
- In a GPT-style model, a position can attend to itself and earlier positions, while future positions are masked out [E6].
- Training can process many positions in parallel while respecting a causal mask, and text generation still proceeds one token at a time [E5].
- Attention allows a word to draw on useful context many sentences earlier, connecting positions directly without following a pronoun chain one mention at a time [E7].

notes.title: Sampling Temperature
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Sampling Temperature controls how random the output is by dividing the next-token scores before applying softmax, affecting the variety of generated text. Lower temperatures favor more likely continuations, while higher temperatures explore more possibilities and raise variance.
DETAILS:
- Temperature is a setting in every API call that controls how "random" the output is [E2].
- Lower temperature settings, such as 0.3, cause the probability distribution to sharpen, leading to fewer surprises and keeping the model on its most probable path [E7].
- Higher temperature settings, such as 1.2, flatten the distribution, causing rarer words to appear more often [E7].
- At temperature 0.3, the model produces samples like "the report about the item explains the price in detail ." [E7].
- At temperature 0.8, the model produces samples like "the report about the car explains the journey in detail ." [E7].
- At temperature 1.2, the model produces samples like "ivy learned that the opposite of slow is fast ." [E7].
- The model is confident enough that at temperatures 0.8 and 1.2, the seeded draw picked identical samples [E7].

notes.title: Prompt Engineering
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Prompt Engineering involves guiding an LLM's output by adding detail, examples, constraints, and formatting requirements to steer the probability of a desired answer. It is crucial to understand that the prompt itself functions as context, and specific prompting techniques help reduce ambiguity and improve model performance.
DETAILS:
- Prompting is described as guidance, where adding detail, examples, constraints, and formatting requirements shrinks the space of acceptable continuations, making the "right" answer more likely [E1].
- Specific prompts work because they reduce ambiguity, leading to lower entropy in the next-token distribution and making the model less likely to wander into the wrong answer shape [E1].
- Users should prompt the model like a tool rather than a colleague, recognizing that the underlying mechanism is a next-token predictor shaped by RLHF [E2].
- Attention failure occurs when a model misses the intent of a prompt, as seen when it latches onto a specific detail like a distance question instead of the overall point [E3].
- Voice-to-Text prompts can help because speech naturally includes more context, allows users to state edge cases, and explains intent rather than just task labels [E4].
- LLMs do not start fresh per message; each new request bundles the conversation history, and the model answers based on this provided context [E5].
- Context is everything; the surrounding context, including system instructions, history, and the latest message, changes the conditional probabilities of next tokens without changing the model's learned weights [E6].
- The prompt is context, and more relevant context gives the model less to guess; the prompt supplies background facts and the ask, and more context means more information relevant to the task [E7].

notes.title: Context Windows
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Context windows define the maximum amount of information, measured in tokens, a model can hold at once, which directly impacts its capacity for processing and memory. Understanding context windows is crucial because they relate to limitations like context rot, the need for compression, and the strategy of placing stable rules in durable locations.
DETAILS:
- A context window is the maximum space a model can hold simultaneously, shared by user messages and the model's replies [E1].
- The context window capacity is measured in tokens, and earlier messages remain in context, meaning the bar does not reset between turns [E1].
- State-of-the-art models like Claude Opus have a context window of 1 million tokens, which can hold content equivalent to the entire Lord of the Rings trilogy [E2].
- Larger context windows allow the model to reason over larger inputs such as entire codebases or full documents at once [E2].
- Increasing context size raises cost and latency, and the model only sees the active context, lacking durable memory unless information is resent [E3].
- Context rot occurs as prompts become cluttered, potentially causing the model to miss, misweight, or contradict existing material, and long chats can become confused [E4].
- When the window fills, compaction is a lossy summarization process that summarizes old conversation into a compact block to free up space [E5].
- System instructions and durable project files are better places for stable rules than long casual conversations because they survive compaction and new chats [E6].

notes.title: Fine-Tuning and LoRA
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Fine-tuning and LoRA are methods used to adapt pretrained models, with fine-tuning permanently reshaping the model's distribution by changing its weights, while LoRA involves training a small add-on matrix (adapter) to nudge the model's behavior, offering a cheaper alternative to full fine-tuning. This distinction is relevant when deciding between prompting, LoRA, and fine-tuning based on cost and desired changes.
DETAILS:
- Fine-tuning shifts which tokens the model considers likely because the weights change, leading to completely different predictions with the same prompt [E1].
- Fine-tuning is expensive and permanent because it changes the model’s weights [E1].
- Prompting is cheap and temporary because it steers the same frozen model [E1].
- RLHF involves a three-stage post-training process: Pretraining (unsupervised), SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning), and RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) [E2].
- Prompting changes the instructions and examples supplied for a request, while fine-tuning changes the model [E4].
- LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) trains a tiny add-on matrix (an “adapter”) instead of updating billions of weights, making it approximately 100 times cheaper than fine-tuning [E5].
- Prompting is reversible and costs ~$0, whereas LoRA costs $100s–$10Ks and allows swapping adapters [E5].
- Full fine-tuning costs $10Ks–$1Ms and is irreversible, whereas prompting is renting and LoRA is a lease with an exit clause [E5].

notes.title: Hallucination
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Hallucination occurs because fluent systems are designed to reward plausible continuation rather than guaranteeing source access or truth verification. This is a system property where plausibility without evidence is the failure mode, and it can arise from normal generation processes.
DETAILS:
- An LLM contains learned statistical structure in its parameters and does not consult a verified, current, cited database unless provided one [E1].
- The next-token objective rewards plausible continuation and does not guarantee source access, truth verification, or current information [E2].
- Probability is not truth; the chart scores possible next tokens, not whether a claim is correct [E2].
- Plausibility without evidence is the failure mode, and grounding the answer in checkable evidence is necessary [E2].
- Retrieval can bring in irrelevant or incorrect material, and a generated citation can be fabricated or fail to support its claim [E3].
- Higher thinking modes can improve reasoning but can still produce an incorrect answer and do not create missing source evidence [E3].
- Lower temperatures concentrate the sampling distribution toward already-likely tokens, which can cause a likely false claim to become more consistently repeated but is not a general factual-accuracy guarantee [E3].

notes.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a method that allows a Large Language Model (LLM) to access external, private data to ground its answers, addressing the limitation that an LLM's knowledge is frozen at its training data. It matters because it enables the use of private knowledge without retraining the model, which grounds answers in evidence and reduces hallucinations.
DETAILS:
- RAG allows an LLM to answer questions based on retrieved documents rather than its internal memory [E4].
- RAG grounds answers in evidence, meaning the model cites retrieved documents, such as a specific revenue figure, instead of guessing [E4].
- RAG enables the use of private knowledge, like company internal documents, by retrieving and injecting it into the prompt without requiring fine-tuning or retraining [E4].
- RAG is used when an LLM searches the web before answering, when a code model reads project files, when a chatbot answers from internal HR docs, or when a support tool pulls answers from a help center [E3].
- The process involves finding relevant information, giving it to the AI with the question, and using external sources, vector matching, context, and an AI answer [E5].
- Chunking text splits long documents into smaller, useful passages, keeping related ideas and their context together so that the question can select relevant pieces to include in the model’s context [E6].
- Vector databases store numerical representations of text called embeddings, and vector search finds chunks near the question by comparing their vector representations, which is used to retrieve passages for the model to read [E7].

notes.title: Local Open Models
notes.raw_output:
SUMMARY: Local Open Models refer to open-weight models that can be run on a student's own hardware, which involves considerations for licensing, local inference setup, and memory calculations. This topic is relevant as it addresses the deployment and operational aspects of open models.
DETAILS:
- Open weights, open source, and local deployment describe different properties of a model. [E4]
- Local inference means the model computation runs on the student’s own hardware. [E4]
- For offline operation, one must download the compatible model and runtime first, select the local model, and ensure tools, embedding models, and other workflow dependencies are local too. [E4]
- Memory calculations use decimal GB and nominal parameter counts: number of parameters × bits per weight ÷ 8. For example, 8 billion weights at 16 bits occupy about 16 GB and at 4 bits about 4 GB before overhead. [E4]
- For full GPU residency, a 32B model’s nominal 16 GB of 4-bit weights leaves no room on a 16 GB GPU for overhead and context. [E4]
- CPU-only inference can work with sufficient system RAM but may be slower. [E4]
